questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I mainly chose UC Berkeley because of its great reputation and academic opportunities, especially within my field of study. The weather in the Bay Area is also super nice, and SF is only a 25-minute train ride away :)

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy, Berkeley is very good at providing resources for almost everything, you just have to know where to find it. Just be sure to check your Berkeley email frequently and attend the orientation meetings before your stay :)

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I attended Golden Bear Orientation (GBO), which gives you an introduction to the Berkeley campus, traditions and values, and gives you the opportunity to meet other students (mostly transfer students) across many different majors. I highly recommend signing up for GBO! Apart from that, it is always possible to receive assistance with anything else from the Berkeley International Office.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Make sure to keep an eye out in your email for a sign up link to GBO so you don't miss out :) They send you a lot (!) of emails, but it is worth at least skimming through them so you don't miss anything important (a lot of people missed GBO because they missed the email)

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
UC Berkeley offers housing in either residence halls (avoid the ones prioritizing freshmen students if you don't want to live with a bunch of 18 year olds) or apartments. They send you emails about how to apply for these.

If you don't go through UC Berkeley to find housing, there are a lot of different choices, and Berkeley can also help you navigate this. I chose International House, which I can highly recommend! You meet a lot of new people (mostly other internationals, but also Americans), and they constantly have fun events that you can attend. Food is included, and the food hall is one of the best (if not the best) on campus. It is, however, quite expensive; you pay around $11,000 for your entire stay there (including the mandatory meal plan).

You can also look into co-ops, which is a way cheaper alternative! However, be aware that the co-ops are not always managed very well, which can cause some issues.

If you look into simply renting an apartment, be aware of scams; they happen a lot every year at Berkeley. Luckily, Berkeley is more than willing to help you with this as well, so if you have any doubts about whether or not an apartment might be a scam, just ask them :)

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer:
It really depends on your housing. 

If you've gotten your housing through UC Berkeley, you will most likely get a meal plan that you can use at various dining halls (and maybe some cafés depending on the meal plan) on and around campus.

If you don't have housing through UC Berkeley, you have more freedom with regards to where and what you eat :) You might still be able to get the meal plans if you want, and should always just be able to go into the dinings halls and pay a flat fee to eat there. If you live at International House, your meal plan is only for the International House dining hall.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: I would say on campus housing gives you the best exchange experience, but it is also more expensive.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Be sure to start early. For example, International House already starts accepting applicants in May.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Course registration is pretty easy, but I would recommend becoming familiar with the website before the day you can register for your classes. You can also add your preferred classes to the "basket" beforehand - then they will be ready for the exact time your course registration opens. I recommend to sit ready at your computer exactly when the course registration opens if you want the best chances at attending your preferred courses, especially if your major is impacted (for example, a lot of Haas Business School classes get filled up really fast). I can also recommend just signing up for more courses than you need - you can always just drop some of them later.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
It is just a website where you can "shop around" and add courses to your basket :) They also have a schedule planner so you can see your schedule with the courses you have chosen.

You are assigned a specific date and time where your courses registration starts. This assigned date and time is not the same for all Berkeley students, so some of the courses might already be partly or fully filled by the time you can register for them. But don't worry, in most cases you should be fine; otherwise, just sign up for the course anyways, as a lot of people on the waitlist get in later on in the add & drop period in the beginning of the semester.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I'm sure you can find lots of resources on the Berkeley website or CalNet :)

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I successfully signed up for all my classes. I was on the waitlist on one of them in the beginning, but got in a few days after I registered.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Apart from what I have mentioned above:

Be sure to become familiar with what the add & drop period is and when it starts and ends.

Again, don't be afraid to register for more courses than you need, as it gives you more flexibility, and you can just drop them later on. I think 20.5 units is the maximum though. You can also just get all the courses your registered for pre-approved by KU, and then just change your pre-approval once you finally have decided on which courses you are taking.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Berkeley offers a wide variety of courses, and the professors are usually good. Be sure to check out DeCal, which are student-run classes on a variety of subjects that are usually around 1-2 units. If you attend College of Letters and Science, you are required by Berkeley to take 13 units, but only 12 units are required by KU, so it is very convenient to be able to take a DeCal for the remaining unit :)

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
I can only talk about economics courses, as this is what I study.

The undergraduate courses are generally not that difficult compared to KU, especially with regards to the math. However, the workload is quite high, as assignments, attendance, midterms etc. also count towards your grade, so you can't be going on too long trips if you want a good grade :)

If you really want to be challenged academically, then choose as many graduate courses as you can.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It was honestly very similar, with big lectures followed by smaller discussions (taught by a PhD student) every week. You have to be way more formal in how you address your professors, but they are generally very willing to help and have lots of office hours.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Environmental Economics (ECON C125)
Public Economics (ECON 131)
Financial Economics (ECON 136)
Foundations of Data Science (DATA C8)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I can recommend all the courses I took.

Public Economics is good, but it is also mainly about the US (whereas other economics courses are about more general theories), so if you don't care at all about the US public sector, I would probably avoid it. I heard that the course is better when it is run by Emmanuel Saez as opposed to Daniel Wilson (Wilson's exams are much more difficult, and he is not a very good lecturer).

Financial Economics is a good course that provides a broad introduction to corporate finance, and it is not too easy or difficult.

Environmental Economics is very interesting, but maybe a bit too easy.

Foundations of Data Science is a really good course if you are completely new to Python. Within computer science and similar majors, it is a very famous course (both at Berkeley and in the US in general), and it is also the biggest course at Berkeley, so it is run extremely well. It is also not too difficult, but the workload is quite high.

Apart from the courses I took, I have heard good things about Money and Banking (ECON 165). It is a very popular course, so be sure to register for it as early as possible.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Nothing really. You can find help with your budget on both the UCEAP and Berkeley website.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: You can save a lot of money by buying something other than SHIP insurance, but be aware that there is a slight risk that UC Berkeley won't accept your third-party insurance and then force you to pay for SHIP anyways. I used something called ISO International Student Health Insurance, which worked for me and the other Danish people who went to Berkeley that semester.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There are a lot of clubs you can join and different sports you can play (no padel tennis yet, unfortunately). Be sure to attend Calapalooza (a student organization fair) in the beginning of the semester.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: They basically have everything you can think of, just check the website.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Going on hikes in the fire trails is really nice, and they offer some great views over Berkeley and the Bay Area. Be sure to watch the sunset from up there one day :)


For going out in Berkeley:

Raleigh's hosts Taco Tuesdays every Tuesday

Tap Haus is pretty nice and has lots of pool tables

Go to Kip's if you want to dance

Be sure to attend a few frat parties too! It is easiest to do it during rush week in the beginning of the semester.


For going out elsewhere:

I mainly went to SF, where I can recommend Monroe SF (really cheap drinks if you come really early (around 5pm) on Fridays), Audio SF if you like EDM, and generally the Cow Hollow/Pacific Heights area for bar hopping.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Around the Bay Area: Sausalito, Muir Woods, Silicon Valley, Stanford, SF of course.

Further away: Santa Cruz, Lake Tahoe, Yosemite, LA, Las Vegas, Grand Canyon.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy, their culture is fairly similar.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
Attend Golden Bear Orientation and attend parties and events, especially in the beginning. International House has many cool events, and you can often attend even if you are not a resident (sometimes you just have to know a resident who can let you in).

You can also join student organizations, but some of them can be pretty difficult joining because you won't be at Berkeley for a very long time.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: None really, but maybe be prepared that random strangers will start talking to you quite a lot. There are also a lot of homeless people in Berkeley and around campus.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Americans are usually very nice and welcoming, so it is super easy to talk to new people and get to know them :)

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Enjoy
2. Your
3. Stay

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Remember that you can ask any questions you have in the Facebook group for KU students going on exchange to UC.

Use the Berkeley Academic Guide when exploring courses.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The people I met there and the many great experiences that we had together :)

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Going home :(

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer:
Remember to start your VISA application pretty early, as it can be a pretty long process, and you don't want it to hinder any other summer vacation plans that you might have.

Also be sure to look into the health requirements in advance. I think you can also fullfill some of them after you have arrived, but I honestly wouldn't waste time on that.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
